name: Psyche
significance: Psyche was launched to investigate a scientific gap that no prior mission could address: since planetary metallic cores are inaccessible everywhere, including on Earth, the metal-rich asteroid 16 Psyche offers a possible directly observable analog to a protoplanet's exposed core, if Psyche is confirmed to be one. It is the first mission to a predominantly metallic body, carrying a magnetometer, gamma-ray/neutron spectrometer, and imagers to map composition, topography, and any remnant magnetic field, an instrument suite never before flown to a metal-dominated target. Ground and space telescope observations conducted before and during the mission's cruise have already revised estimates of Psyche's bulk metal content downward from earlier assumptions, suggesting a more porous, mixed metal-rock body rather than a solid iron-nickel mass. The spacecraft is still en route, with orbital operations at Psyche not beginning until 2029, so the central question, whether Psyche is truly a stripped planetary core or a metal-rich rubble pile formed some other way, remains open.
statusNote: Orbital study of a metal-rich asteroid believed to be part of a planetesimal's core. Single Mars gravity-assist flyby, completed 2026-05-15 at 4,609 km altitude; this leg uses the patched-conic roll-angle solver (like BepiColombo/PSP), not a plain endpoint-anchored arc. Asteroid gravity capture expected 2029-07 (science orbit begins 2029-08); this file uses 2029-07-31 as a representative arrival date pending a firmer published one -- combined with the approximate date, the solved trajectory currently lands ~0.3 AU from Psyche's actual position at that date, larger than this simulator's other patched-conic legs. Worth revisiting once ESA/NASA publish a firmer encounter date closer to arrival.

legs._comment: Real Psyche trajectory (JPL Horizons, target -255, checked 2026-07) sweeps close to a full lap (~345 degrees) around the Sun on this cruise to Mars, reaching ~2.6 AU near 2025-01 (past Mars, into the asteroid belt) before curving back in for the flyby -- close enough to 360 degrees that a plain 2-point Lambert solve misreads it as a small-angle short hop, producing an unconstrained a=1.92 AU / e=0.88 orbit. Split through two real recorded positions so each third stays under 180 degrees of sweep.
